easa.q: ____ is the rate of motion in a particular direction in relation to time.
easa.explain: Velocity is speed with a direction; EASA distinguishes it clearly from speed.

easa.q: When fluid flowing through a tube reaches a constriction, the speed of the fluid ____ and the pressure of the fluid ____.
The boundary layer is the part of the airflow that is ____ to the surface of the aircraft.
easa.explain: The boundary layer is the air closest to the surface (EASA p. 2.4).

easa.q: The ____ of a wing is the width of the wing from the leading edge apex to the trailing edge.
easa.explain: Span runs tip to tip; the chord runs along the stream.

easa.q: A comparison between the wingspan and the chord of a wing is known as ____.
____ is defined as the angle between the chord line of the wing and the direction of the relative wind.
easa.explain: AOA is measured against the relative wind, while incidence is measured against the fuselage datum.

easa.q: ____ drag is generated by the mixing of airflow streamlines between airframe components such as the wing and fuselage.
easa.explain: Two components meeting (wing-fuselage) add interference drag.

easa.q: What type of drag continually increases as airspeed increases?
easa.explain: Induced drag falls with speed; parasite drag rises.

anderson.q: An airfoil at 12° angle of attack has normal and axial force coefficients of 1.2 and 0.03. The lift coefficient is:
anderson.explain: c_l = c_n cos α − c_a sin α.
anderson.detail: c_l = 1.2 cos 12° − 0.03 sin 12° = 1.168; c_d = 1.2 sin 12° + 0.03 cos 12° = 0.279. The sign of the second term is the usual slip.

anderson.q: A low-speed open-circuit wind tunnel has an inlet-to-throat area ratio of 12 and a mercury manometer difference of 10 cm (ρ_Hg = 1.36×10⁴ kg/m³, ρ = 1.23 kg/m³). The test-section velocity is:
anderson.detail: Δp = ρ_Hg g h = 13342 N/m²; V₂ = √[2Δp/(ρ(1 − (A₂/A₁)²))] = 147.8 m/s. Dropping the (1 − 1/144) factor changes the result by only about 0.35%.

anderson.q: A Pitot tube on an aircraft at standard sea level (p = 1.01×10⁵ N/m², ρ = 1.23 kg/m³) reads 1.07×10⁵ N/m². The aircraft speed is:
anderson.detail: V = √[2(1.07×10⁵ − 1.01×10⁵)/1.23] = √[9756] = 98.8 m/s ≈ 192 kt. Typical slips are forgetting the factor 2 or the square root.

anderson.q: At a point on the wing of the aircraft in Problem 3.6 the local velocity is 130 m/s. The pressure coefficient C_p there is:
anderson.detail: C_p = 1 − (130/98.77)² = -0.732. Negative means pressure below the free stream, as expected on a suction surface.

anderson.q: A NACA 2412 airfoil with a 2 m chord at 50 m/s at standard sea level has a lift per unit span of 1353 N/m (ρ = 1.23). The lift coefficient and angle of attack (from the NACA 2412 c_l table of Problem 1.6) are:
anderson.explain: c_l = L'/(q c), then read α from the table.

anderson.q: A thin symmetric airfoil at 1.5° angle of attack. From thin-airfoil theory c_l and c_m,LE are respectively:
anderson.detail: α = 1.5° = 0.02618 rad so c_l = 2π·α = 0.1645. The centre of pressure of a thin symmetric airfoil is at c/4, so c_m,LE = −c_l/4 = -0.0411.

anderson.q: NACA 2412: at α = −6° c_l = −0.39 and c_m,c/4 = −0.045; at α = 4° c_l = 0.65 and c_m,c/4 = −0.037. The aerodynamic centre x_ac/c is:
anderson.detail: dc_m/dc_l = (−0.037 + 0.045)/(0.65 + 0.39) = 0.00769; h_ac = 0.25 − 0.00769 = 0.2423. The aerodynamic centre is almost at the quarter chord.

anderson.q: A NACA 2412 airfoil of 2 m chord flies at 60 m/s at a standard altitude of 3 km (ρ = 0.9093 kg/m³) with α = 4° (c_l = 0.65). The lift per unit span is:
anderson.detail: ρ(3 km) = 0.9091 kg/m³ from ISA; q = 1636.4 N/m²; L' = 1636.4×2×0.65 = 2127 N/m. Using sea-level density instead of 3 km density shifts the result by about 35%.

generated.q: An aircraft keeps the same C_L and air density; speed rises from 100 kt to 200 kt. What happens to lift?
generated.explain: L ∝ V²; EASA gives exactly this example in the Lift section.

generated.q: A wing has a 12 m span and 20 m² area. Its aspect ratio AR is:
Everything else equal, increasing the wing AR makes induced drag:
generated.explain: C_Di = C_L²/(π e AR): larger AR gives smaller C_Di.

generated.q: The pressure at the stagnation point of a free stream equals:
generated.explain: The flow is brought fully to rest, so all the dynamic pressure becomes static pressure.

generated.q: A pressure coefficient C_p = −1 occurs at a point where the local velocity equals:
What is the main effect of ice left on the wing before take-off?
opts: No effect if the layer is thin
generated.explain: A rough surface degrades the boundary layer (EASA p. 2.9); even thin ice is dangerous.

generated.q: For a thin symmetric airfoil in theory the centre of pressure lies at:
generated.explain: A thin symmetric airfoil has its centre of pressure at the aerodynamic centre, c/4 (Anderson 4.7–4.9).

generated.q: Compared with a laminar boundary layer, a turbulent one usually:
opts: is the same in every respect
has more friction but separates later
has less friction and separates later
has less friction and separates sooner
generated.explain: A turbulent layer carries more momentum near the wall so it clings better, at the price of higher skin friction.
